title.value: SARS-CoV-2 infection in Africa: a systematic review and meta-analysis of standardised seroprevalence studies, from January 2020 to December 2021
title.justification: The title is directly taken from the paper and clearly represents the content of the study which is focused on SARS-CoV-2 seroprevalence in Africa.
title.quote: SARS-­CoV-­2 infection in Africa: a systematic review and meta-­analysis of standardised seroprevalence studies, from January 2020 to December 2021

extractions.description: This paper presents a systematic review and meta-analysis of seroprevalence studies conducted in Africa to estimate the seroprevalence of SARS-CoV-2 from January 2020 to December 2021. It highlights the challenges in detecting COVID-19 incidence in Africa due to limited surveillance and lab capacities. The study aims to inform public health decision-making by understanding the population's exposure and guiding targeted public health policies.

primary_category.justification: The paper focuses on the epidemiological assessment of SARS-CoV-2 in Africa and does not directly align with any of the eco-responsible categories since it deals with public health rather than environmental sustainability or climate change issues.
primary_category.quote: Estimating COVID-­19 cumulative incidence in Africa remains problematic due to challenges in contact tracing, routine surveillance systems and laboratory testing capacities and strategies.

secondary_categories.justification: The study focuses on Africa, detailing the seroprevalence and epidemiological data, which can aid public health strategies in regions that typically have less access to resources and data-driven insights.
secondary_categories.quote: Africa is experiencing unprecedented challenges due to the COVID-­19 pandemic, both directly and from the compounding effects of other health, economic and social factors.

primary_sub_category.justification: There is no sub-category that appropriately matches the focus of the paper, which is centered on COVID-19 seroprevalence and public health strategies in Africa.
primary_sub_category.quote: We undertook a meta-­analysis of population-­based seroprevalence studies to estimate SARS-­CoV-­2 seroprevalence in Africa to inform evidence-­based decision making on public health and social measures (PHSM) and vaccine strategy.

secondary_sub_categories.justification: The research aims to provide data that informs evidence-based decision-making and guides public health policies for better health management in Africa, aligning with shared knowledge in global south support.
secondary_sub_categories.quote: We aimed to better understand SARS-CoV-2 epidemiology in Africa up to and before the emergence of the Omicron variant... to inform evidence-based decision making on public health and social measures (PHSM) and vaccine strategy.

applications.value: Inform public health and vaccination strategies in Africa
applications.justification: The study aims to enhance understanding of COVID-19 spread in Africa and guide tailored public health and vaccination strategies.
applications.quote: targeted PHSM and vaccination strategies need to be tailored to local epidemiological situations.

new_primary_category.justification: The study is primarily concerned with understanding public health dynamics in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic in Africa.
new_primary_category.quote: Estimating COVID-­19 cumulative incidence in Africa remains problematic due to challenges in contact tracing, routine surveillance systems and laboratory testing capacities and strategies.

new_primary_sub_category.justification: The paper focuses on seroprevalence and variations across Africa, significantly contributing to the epidemiological analysis of infectious diseases.
new_primary_sub_category.quote: Our primary objectives were to: (1) estimate SARS-­CoV-­2 seroprevalence and changes over time in Africa as a whole and by UN subregions, (2) estimate the extent of undetected infections by comparing seroprevalence and cumulative incidence of confirmed cases and (3) identify heterogeneity in seroprevalence attributable to demographic factors, country-­level factors and study design.
